title: Record your gameplay and feed it to your agents...
author: crackedpotstudio
selftext:
I recently let Claude Code create a small work in progress trailer of my game in Godot. After some prompts and attempts I stumbled on an actual bug in my gameplay, I pointed to the timeframe, explained what I was experiencing and how I want it to be...

I've noticed the result was actually really good, and instead of me tinkering with Claude for a few minutes actually turned into Claude one shotting the solution in 20 seconds... The past few days my workflow evolved from me playing the game and discussing with Claude what I want, to playing my game and recording it and showing it to Claude to actually write different scenarios. And now I actually let Claude play my game following a pre set scenario and recording it. I review the footage and relay back some improvements.

I've noticed that the speed and quality of my improvements and Claude Code sessions has greatly improved and would like to share that tip with this community.

Also I'm curious about the experience of this community with relaying back gameplay feedback to your AI.

comments.author: Carter5on
comments.body: You can grant access to the agent to play and record the game for you. This way you don't need to setup any other software and the recordings are in top quality.

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body: Yeah that's what I'm actually doing now :)

replies.author: CrowdGoesWildWoooo
replies.body: It’s way too slow. Unless you are playing strategy games, it’s not that viable.

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body: Well in my case it’s an farming game so speed isn’t the biggest issue. But I can certainly see it as an problem when testing an action game, fair point!

replies.author: Arcodiant
replies.body: It works for me at around 13-14 parallel projects; the agent has a modding framework for creating the situations it needs to test, as well as scripting so it can bounce around and run multiple tests in a single session. But you definitely have to rein it in so it isn't spending 12 hours playtestong each change.

replies.author: MrLizardsWizard
replies.body: My workflow (all set up with AI) is that when I start my game it automatically turns on OBS to record screen and audio, whisper flow then transcribes the audio track right away, AI takes the content and then comes up with proposalsor fixes based on my feedback and if I say "that's a bug" or anything like that it screenshots the video based on the timestamp of my audio to investigate it.

replies.author: Carter5on
replies.body: I didn't know it could do that and I didn't think about it. Thank you.

comments.author: Academic-Bench-8828
comments.body:
This is not really a great idea. You're going to use a ton of API credits this way. My simulated game tests spit out ASCII character receipts of the game board that the llm can review More cheaply . 
But having an LM review video content seems wildly expensive

replies.author: PastaSaladOverdose
replies.body:
Boom, exactly. 

People - if you want to save tokens force the model to code a tool that can run locally. Once the tool is completed it's assumed that the workload goes through your PC, not reporting back to Claude servers and destroying your usage limit.

replies.author: Academic-Bench-8828
replies.body: I have found that this technique works really really well for finding regressions. Your tests only assert things in a narrow way, but I have my tests dump ASCII maps of levels directly along with the test results so when the llm's reviewing it, it sees not only the assertions which pass and failed. The whole map and any other bugs that can easily be visually debugged when seeing on a 2d map. It works well for a human but even better for an llm because it can do it at scale

replies.author: PastaSaladOverdose
replies.body:
You're absolutely correct in your logic. Breaking down the test case into its simplest form that the LLM can consume is, in my opinion, the correct way to go about it.

The LLM does not need to "see" the game being played like a human. It simply needs a limited data set to compare and contrast. These things are not human, they're super computers. Data rules all.

replies.author: Academic-Bench-8828
replies.body: More and more, my engineering is focused on using llm's most effectively. I'm no longer even worried about the code itself, I'm worried about how well I can write code in the future. My work is more focused on keeping llm costs down and making sure my llm strategies are optimal. But the code itself is fading into the background

replies.author: PastaSaladOverdose
replies.body:
I agree 100%. I've been coding for 20 years. I thought I'd be missing writing the code, but honestly, the more and more I am "vibe coding" I'm realizing that the code was always a pain in the ass and the hardest part of my job..

I realized that I actually enjoy the process more than the code. And these LLMs are allowing me to dive deeper into the process as opposed to the code and for the first time in a long time I'm getting a ton of fulfillment and enjoyment out of creating again.

replies.author: Academic-Bench-8828
replies.body: I wish I could say that unemployment has not been fun, but the free time has let me explore llm development without the overhead of work. I am burning through my savings trying to finish my projects but I'm having a lot of fun doing it. I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do after this, I'm writing super genius level code but no one will hire me to even write a react website anymore

replies.author: PastaSaladOverdose
replies.body:
Brother, I am in the exact same boat. I am landing interviews like crazy, getting to final rounds, but at the end of the day I'm up until 1-2am working on personal projects. 

My drive and interest is exponentially growing every day. I am skilling up incredibly fast with AI assisted development. I'm working towards Claude certifications through their online courses... But I can't take the cert tests unless I am sponsored by a company that's certified through Claude.

A lot of this AI related knowledge is being gatekept like crazy. Entry level AI jobs don't even exist. Employers have no idea how to use AI, hire for AI, or scale to it. 

It's a fucking mess.

replies.author: Scott-Whittaker
replies.body:
Same here. Over 20 years as a web developer, now unemployed and trying to stay afloat while pouring most of my time into using Claude for personal projects. 

The possibility space feels wide open, and Claude is productivity cocaine. If I can just figure out how to find a niche project that I’ll enjoy working on and an audience to support it I can finally opt out of the rat race. 

But I can’t keep this up for too much longer, I’m coming up on 2 years unemployed and one financial disaster away from ruin.

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body: Very interesting thread with some solid info, thanks for your input!

comments.author: dank_summers
comments.body: I recently set up my agent to play the game on headless Godot setup. Feel like the video aspect would just eat token for no reason

comments.author: TwiGGorized
comments.body: Do you direct it to the point of the recording or can claude just parse the whole information of the recording?

comments.author: dantemp
comments.body:
One of the first thing I made my Claude do is create a replay system for my game, so I can tell it "in my last game at the 34th second my character got stuck, figure out why", it's been very good for fixing bugs. 

The replays are a log of commands and seeds so they are very light and very quick to load.

comments.author: SaintFX
comments.body:
I make sure that the local save contains as much telemetry as possible and then as I’m testing I’ll have Claude pull the save from my phone and check it against our stated goals. It can even do it remotely as long as I’m on my network that my Claude session is running on.

This allows me to give it feedback as I’m playing - like this part is taking too long, this is too easy, etc and it can pull the save and see what’s going on and make adjustments.

Obviously I might play it differently than my users but it at least gives a baseline to work against and then we come up with different player personas to simulate with.

comments.author: max13007
comments.body:
I added a "bug report" button to all of my projects (games or software) - it automatically takes a screenshot (if possible), and logs relevant game/log data at the time of hitting the button. 

Lets me playtest for much longer, queue up a long list of changes/bugs/etc... then i just go back to CC and say: "Bugfix pass please" and we're off. It's less resource-heavy than having it playtest itself or FFMPEG video for analysis.

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body: I have an agent for bug and stress testing, it fires up Godot headless and runs a bunch of scenarios and tries to break stuff when I ask it to, it also checks if old savefiles are still compatible. The video feedback is mainly for gameplay improvements. Like “make this gate open automatically” or something like “smooth out this pathing option in the building menu”

replies.author: max13007
replies.body:
> Like “make this gate open automatically” or something like “smooth out this pathing option in the building menu”

What I suggested works very well for this, for what it's worth. Don't get me wrong, if you've got a system that works, that's what's most important. 

However, if it's still the way it was a few weeks back, LLMs can't watch videos, so they use FFMPEG or something similar to convert the video into PNGs, then analyze frame-by-frame/frame sampling. I will still use recordings if there's something very specific it's not able to see in a screenshot, but using a single screenshot will burn usage less than analyzing a whole video.

replies.author: loki_nz
replies.body: This is the way. Capture the game logs, current state + screen shot and an optional note. This and a tuning panel that I can tweak just about any variable in game and save it.

comments.author: hydroxyHU
comments.body:
I asked Claude to build a logging system that records my decisions during playthroughs, so I can have it analyze them later. I also created a simulation bot to make sure new mechanics or balance changes don’t make the game significantly easier or harder.  
It’s far from perfect, of course, but it’s a useful point of reference that helps me track how the game’s balance evolves over time and in which direction changes are pushing it.

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body: I've done it before when lazy, it works great but not worth the token cost. Specifically I'd record maybe a 10min playtest and make verbal notes on changes or bugs so Claude can just make sure to screenshot around those timings. It definitely works, and it's nice that I don't have to prompt and make more decisions back and forth. I still think I prefer just play testing and then reporting back to iterate.

replies.author: Bonelessgummybear
replies.body: Just reflected on the past 2 days of development. 26 million tokens burned and the biggest cost was frame grabs and screenshot reading.

comments.author: Alone-Biscotti6145
comments.body:
Not the move you think unfortunately you are better off doing screenshots. Claude is not a video model, it has vision but only static. Pretty much plays your video like a flipbook and misses a ton of detail. If you use ffmpg it is a bit better and has broader control.

Only the frontier video model is Gemini, but unless you're using Argon or Pro, Gemini is not strong enough as a main coder IMHO.

replies.author: QTpopOfficial
replies.body:
While I don't disagree with the facts of what you're saying, such as the whole It can't technically watch a video.

If you dictate properly, it does a stupid good job of clipping out that section, yanking screenshots it needs, then fixing whatever the hell it is. 

Been worth it for me. More so if its something I can replicate and talk through.

replies.author: Alone-Biscotti6145
replies.body: I can agree with this if you're using it to pull specific screenshots. It works well, but don't rely on it to catch everything with video.

replies.author: QTpopOfficial
replies.body:
It’s been super useful for movement related things actually. It’ll take a few snapshots then use my dictation with them to sort stuff. 

It’s pulling entire sections fwiw.

replies.author: 3skull
replies.body: I do a single pic and mark the area for it to look at works wonders with unreal engine zone graph issues

comments.body: That’s probably a nature of my game but basically all needed info is already known to Claude through mcp in form of combat log. Added text context can help to point out what got wrong, and screenshots capture UI bugs
